fetched_contents.text: Brain stem strokes can have complex symptoms and can be hard to diagnose. A person may have vertigo, dizziness and severe imbalance without the hallmark of most strokes — weakness on one side of the body. Vertigo dizziness symptoms or imbalance usually occur together; dizziness alone is not a sign of stroke. A brain stem stroke can also cause double vision, slurred speech and decreased consciousness. Only a half-inch in diameter, the brain stem controls all basic activities of the central nervous system: consciousness, blood pressure and breathing. All motor control for the body flows through it. Brain stem strokes can impair any or all these functions. More severe brain stem strokes can cause locked-in syndrome, a condition in which survivors can move only their eyes. If a stroke in the brain stem results from a clot, the faster blood flow can be restored, the better the chances for recovery. Like all strokes, brain stem strokes produce a wide spectrum of deficits and recovery. Whether a survivor has minor or severe deficits depends on the location of the stroke within the brain stem, the extent of injury and how quickly treatment is provided. Risk factors for brain stem stroke are the same as for strokes in other areas of the brain: high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease, atrial fibrillation and smoking. Similarly, brain stem strokes can be caused by a clot or a hemorrhage. Rare causes include injury to an artery due to sudden head or neck movements. Recovery is possible. Because brain stem strokes don’t usually affect language ability, the patient is often able to participate more fully in rehabilitation. Double vision and vertigo usually resolve after several weeks of recovery in mild to moderate brain stem strokes.

fetched_contents.text: Causes of Double Vision A range of conditions can cause double vision, including problems within the eye, such as the cornea or lens. Other underlying causes can involve muscles or nerves controlling eye function and movement, or issues in the brain. Some causes can be minor, such as astigmatism, or life threatening, such as an aneurysm or stroke. Read more about double vision diagnosis. Double Vision Caused by Cornea Problems The cornea is the clear layer that covers the front of the eye. Its main function is to focus incoming light into the eye. Problems in the cornea distort its surface, which can create double vision. Such problems include: * Astigmatism * Dry eyes * Infections such as shingles or herpes zoster * Scars caused by disease, injury or infection Double Vision Caused by Lens Problems Your eye's lens works with the cornea to focus incoming light onto the retina (back of the eye). The lens is behind the pupil and changes shape as it focuses. The most common lens problem that can cause double vision is a cataract, a clouding of the normally clear lens due to aging. Our eye surgeons can remove cataracts in an outpatient surgery. Learn more about cataract surgery. Double Vision Caused by Eye Muscle Problems Six muscles in your eye socket control your eye's movement up, down, to each side and in rotation. Problems in these extraocular muscles include weakness or paralysis that prevent one eye from moving in coordination with the other. Eye muscle problems include: * Graves' disease, a thyroid condition that affects eye muscles and causes vertical double vision, in which one image appears above the other * Strabismus (misaligned eyes), a weakened or paralyzed eye muscle that prevents the eyes from aligning properly Double Vision Caused by Nerve Problems Certain cranial nerves connect the brain to the eye muscles to control eye movement. Some conditions that can affect or damage these cranial nerves and lead to double vision include: * Diabetes, a metabolic disease affecting your body's ability to process blood sugar that can cause nerve damage * Guillain-Barre syndrome, a nerve condition in which early symptoms can occur in the eyes, causing muscle weakness * Myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks neuromuscular junctions involved in eye movement * Multiple sclerosis, a chronic neurological disease affecting the central nervous system, possibly damaging nerves that control eye movement Double Vision Caused by Brain Problems Several areas inside the brain process visual information that is transmitted from the eyes through nerves. If these areas are affected by illness or injury, double vision can result. Some brain conditions that can lead to double vision include: * Brain aneurysm * Brain tumor * Migraine headache * Pressure inside the brain from bleeding, infection or trauma * Stroke Double Vision Caused by Giant Cell Arteritis Giant Cell Arteritis, also known as Temporal Arteritis, occurs when the arteries near the temples became inflamed, leading to reduced blood flow. When these vessels, which are responsible for eye nourishment, encounter reduced blood flow a condition known as anterior ischemic optic neuropathy can develop. Vision and other symptoms include: * Vision Loss * Blurred vision * Double vision * Dizziness * Persistent headaches * Fatigue Read more about double vision treatment.

fetched_contents.text: Transient ischaemic attack (TIA) - NHS The symptoms of a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) are the same as those of a stroke, but they only last for a few minutes or hours. Recognising the signs of a TIA Like a stroke, the signs and symptoms of a TIA usually begin suddenly. It’s important to recognise the symptoms quickly and call 999 to ask for an ambulance straight away. The main symptoms can be remembered with the word FAST: * Face – the face may have dropped on 1 side, the person may not be able to smile, or their mouth or eye may have drooped. * Arms – the person may not be able to lift both arms and keep them there, because of weakness or numbness in one arm. * Speech – their speech may be slurred or garbled, or the person may not be able to talk at all, despite appearing to be awake; they may also have problems understanding what you're saying to them. * Time – it's time to call 999 immediately if you notice any of these signs or symptoms. It's important for everyone to be aware of these signs and symptoms. If you live with or care for someone in a high-risk group, such as an older person or someone with diabetes or high blood pressure, being aware of the symptoms is even more important. Other possible symptoms The symptoms in the FAST test identify most strokes and TIAs, but a TIA can occasionally cause different symptoms that typically appear suddenly (usually over a few seconds). Other signs and symptoms may include: * complete paralysis of one side of the body * sudden vision loss, blurred vision or double vision * vertigo * being sick * dizziness * confusion * difficulty understanding what others are saying * problems with balance and co-ordination * difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) However, there may be other causes for these symptoms. When to get medical advice Call 999 immediately and ask for an ambulance if you or someone else has symptoms of a TIA or stroke. Even if the symptoms disappear while you're waiting for an ambulance to arrive, an assessment in hospital should still be done. You should be referred to see a specialist within 24 hours of the start of your symptoms. A TIA is a warning that you're at risk of having a full stroke in the near future. An assessment can help doctors determine the best way to reduce the chances of this happening. If you think you've had a TIA previously, but the symptoms have since passed and you did not get medical advice at the time, make an urgent appointment with a GP. They can refer you for a hospital assessment, if appropriate. Page last reviewed: 28 June 2023 Next review due: 28 June 2026

## Non-emergency but still important differential diagnoses

The evidence points to several systemic and ophthalmologic causes that may explain double vision but are not immediately life-threatening, yet still require prompt evaluation. These conditions are important because they can be treatable, chronic, or require early intervention to avoid complications, and they often involve tests like eye exams or imaging.

### Systemic and ophthalmologic causes that may still need prompt evaluation

The strongest non-emergency but still important causes are **Graves’ disease/Graves’ orbitopathy**, **diabetes**, **thyroid eye disease**, **cervical spondylosis**, and **other treatable chronic conditions**. The evidence explicitly states that **Graves’ disease can result in a special eye misalignment** and that **Graves’ orbitopathy can cause double vision**, ranging from mild to severe and temporary to permanent [N2-R2], [N2-R3], [N2-R5]. It also notes that **diabetes can cause nerve damage** and that **Graves’ disease, myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome** are conditions that can affect cranial nerves and eye movement [N2-F2]. 

A second relevant source emphasizes that **double vision can be a red flag of serious health conditions** but is **usually a temporary issue** and advises visiting an eye care specialist as soon as possible [N4-R2]. This supports the idea that some causes are not immediately life-threatening, yet still merit prompt specialist evaluation.

### When the symptoms could be related to a chronic or treatable condition

The evidence supports the possibility of **chronic or treatable conditions**. **Graves’ disease** is clearly an autoimmune condition that may cause persistent or fluctuating double vision [N2-R2], [N2-R5]. **Diabetes** is presented as a systemic metabolic disease that can cause nerve damage [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic source also notes that diplopia can be **short-term** and that it is important to see a healthcare provider right away if changes in vision occur [N5-F4]. That wording is consistent with a chronic or treatable cause that still needs timely care rather than emergency treatment.

### Whether tests like eye exams or imaging are likely to be needed

The evidence indicates that tests are likely to be needed. The **Stanford Health Care** source says that causes of double vision include problems within the eye, such as the cornea or lens, and that other underlying causes can involve muscles, nerves, or brain issues [N2-F2]. That implies that an eye exam is a reasonable starting point, especially if the cause is intraocular or extraocular. 

The **Cleveland Clinic** source also says to **visit your eye care specialist as soon as you notice any changes in your vision** [N6-R1], and the **Cleveland Clinic diplopia article** states that diplopia should be evaluated promptly, especially if it occurs suddenly [N5-F4]. The **TIA/stroke-related sources** also emphasize that sudden double vision with red-flag symptoms should trigger emergency care, but they do not suggest that imaging is unnecessary for non-emergency causes [N3-F3]. 

In summary, the most important non-emergency differential diagnoses are **Graves’ disease**, **diabetes**, **thyroid eye disease**, **myasthenia gravis**, and other chronic or treatable conditions affecting eye muscles, nerves, or the brain. These usually require **prompt eye evaluation** and may involve **imaging or specialist testing** if the cause is unclear, but they are not the same as life-threatening conditions requiring immediate emergency care [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F2][N4-R2][N5-F4].

## Most likely urgent causes and their clinical urgency

The evidence strongly supports that the patient’s symptoms are highly urgent. The most likely urgent causes are **brainstem stroke**, **TIA (transient ischemic attack)**, **stroke with visual or balance symptoms**, and **acute brain lesions or aneurysms**. The urgency is clear: these are **life-threatening**, **neurological emergencies**, and **require immediate care**.

### Which conditions explain both double vision and unsteadiness

The evidence shows that **brainstem stroke** is the most direct explanation for both **double vision** and **unsteadiness**. The **American Stroke Association** source states that a brainstem stroke can cause **double vision, slurred speech, and decreased consciousness** [N1-F1]. Another source says that **brainstem stroke can also cause double vision, slurred speech, and decreased consciousness** [N1-R3]. The **stroke.org** page also says that a brainstem stroke can cause **double vision, slurred speech, and decreased consciousness** [N1-R1]. The **NHS TIA/stroke** source lists **sudden vision loss, blurred vision, or double vision** among possible symptoms, along with **vertigo** and **dizziness** [N3-R1]. It also notes that **stroke warning signs include sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, slurred speech, and balance problems** [N3-R3].

The evidence also suggests that **TIA** can explain both **double vision and balance issues**. The **NHS TIA article** states that **sudden vision loss, blurred vision, or double vision** can occur with a TIA [N3-R1]. The **Yale Medicine** article says that **double vision, loss of vision in one or both eyes, balance problems, and other symptoms are urgent TIA and stroke symptoms** [N3-R2]. The **Memphis Neurology** blog likewise notes that **problems such as blurred/double vision or temporary blindness in one or both eyes often accompany a TIA** [N3-R4]. 

In addition, **stroke affecting the vision centers of the brain** can cause **loss of sight in one eye, double vision, or inability to see one half of the world** [N1-R4]. This supports the idea that **stroke-related visual or balance symptoms** are the most likely urgent explanation for both double vision and unsteadiness.

### Which conditions are life-threatening and require immediate care

The evidence repeatedly treats these conditions as **life-threatening emergencies**. **Brainstem stroke** is described as **a medical emergency** and **a leading cause of death** [N1-R3]. The **stroke.org** source also states that **brainstem stroke can have complex symptoms and can be hard to diagnose**, and that **only a half-inch in diameter, the brain stem controls all basic activities of the central nervous system** [N1-F1]. That underscores the life-threatening nature of brainstem stroke.

**TIA** is also treated as **as urgent as a stroke** in the **Yale Medicine** source [N3-R2]. The **NHS TIA article** says that if the symptoms are **slurred speech, weakness, or numbness on one side of the body, double vision, loss of vision in one or both eyes, balance**, or other stroke-like symptoms, you should **call 999 immediately** [N3-R2]. The **NHS TIA/stroke** source also says that **sudden numbness, confusion, vision loss, dizziness, and severe headache are all signs of stroke** [N3-R5].

The evidence also treats **acute brain lesions** and **aneurysms** as serious and potentially life-threatening. The **Stanford Health Care** source says that double vision can be caused by **brain aneurysm or stroke** [N2-F2], while the **Diplopia** article lists **stroke, intracerebral aneurysms, brain tumors, and giant cell arteritis** as important and common causes [N2-R4]. Although **giant cell arteritis** is less immediately life-threatening than stroke or aneurysm, it is still a serious condition that can cause vision loss and requires urgent evaluation [N2-F2].

### What symptoms are most concerning and should trigger emergency response

The most concerning symptoms are those that match the **FAST warning signs** or other stroke/TIA red flags. The evidence says that **sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body**, **slurred or confused speech**, **sudden vision loss, blurred vision, or double vision**, **vertigo**, **dizziness**, **being sick**, **confusion**, **difficulty understanding what others are saying**, and **problems with balance and coordination** are all signs of stroke or TIA [N3-F3]. It also emphasizes that **face drooping, arm weakness, speech changes, and time to call 999** are the key signs to recognize [N3-F3].

In the patient’s case, the symptoms that most strongly trigger emergency response are:
- **Double vision**
- **Unsteadiness or balance problems**
- **Extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk**

These are consistent with the **brainstem stroke** and **TIA** urgency signals in the evidence [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The **Facebook/MedCenterHealth** source also states that **dizziness plus one other symptom can signal stroke**, and the **Cleveland Clinic** source says to call 911 or go to the emergency room immediately if double vision comes with emergency signs like **severe headache, weakness, or slurred speech** [N4-R5]. 

### Bottom line

The most likely urgent causes are **brainstem stroke**, **TIA**, and **stroke-related visual or balance symptoms**. These are **life-threatening conditions** that require **immediate care**. The most concerning symptoms are **double vision**, **unsteadiness**, **balance problems**, **slurred speech**, **numbness or weakness on one side**, **dizziness**, and **vision changes**. The evidence supports treating these symptoms as a **medical emergency** and calling emergency services immediately [N1-F1][N1-R3][N3-F3][N3-R2][N4-R5].

It also says not to panic and to find a safe place if sudden double vision or dizziness happens [N4-R3]. So the patient should explain the problem clearly and honestly, while staying calm.

You can reassure the patient that it’s important to treat this seriously, but not overly alarming. The evidence supports the idea that double vision can be scary, and that it is usually short-term, but it also emphasizes that prompt evaluation is still needed [N5-F4]. - “This is a sign that something may be wrong, and it’s important to get help quickly.”

The evidence also says that double vision can be a red flag of serious conditions, but it is usually a short-term issue [N4-R2]. That wording is useful because it gives reassurance that the symptoms may not mean the worst-case scenario, while still emphasizing urgency.

### How to ask the doctor for the most important tests

The evidence supports asking the doctor for tests that can rule out stroke, TIA, brainstem stroke, and other serious causes. The most important tests likely to be asked for include:
- **Eye exam** to assess the cause of double vision [N2-F2][N6-R1]

### Bottom line

In simple terms:  
- **Tell the doctor exactly what happened** and what symptoms you have.  
- **Ask for tests that can rule out stroke, TIA, brainstem stroke, or other serious causes**.
